analysis.one_liner: Strips FDA authority over foods and supplements, letting makers make drug-like health claims.
analysis.headline: The bill never left a House subcommittee and died when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003, without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten the definition of a "drug" in federal food and drug law so that foods and dietary supplements no longer counted as drugs. That would remove the Food and Drug Administration's power to treat a food or supplement as a drug — meaning makers could state that their products treat, prevent, or cure diseases without going through the drug approval process of clinical trials and FDA review. Supporters cast this as giving consumers more information; the practical effect is that health claims on foods and supplements could be made without government verification.
analysis.who_benefits: Dietary supplement and food manufacturers, who could market products as treating or preventing disease without paying for drug approval, running clinical trials, or facing FDA action for unapproved drug claims.

how_it_helps.text: Amends the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act to exclude food, including dietary supplements, from the definition of "drug."
Sponsors described the purpose as allowing consumers greater access to information regarding the health benefits of foods and dietary supplements.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers, who would face health claims on foods and supplements that no longer have to meet the evidence standards the FDA applies to drugs, and the FDA, which would lose a tool for policing products marketed as cures.

drawbacks.text: Without the drug definition applying to foods and supplements, a food or supplement could be marketed as treating or curing a disease without the clinical trials the FDA requires of actual drugs, leaving consumers with no government-verified basis for those claims.
The FDA would lose its ability to act against a food or supplement sold as an unapproved new drug, removing one of the main enforcement paths for products making medical claims.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Supporters argue that the change frees up truthful information about foods and supplements that current law suppresses, since even accurate health claims can trigger drug rules. The cost is that the claims no longer have to be proven: the drug approval process is the mechanism that requires clinical evidence before a treatment claim reaches consumers, and this bill removes that requirement for every food and supplement. Consumers gain access to more claims and lose the assurance behind them.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then its Health subcommittee, where nothing happened before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ron Paul introduced the bill on June 21, 2001, with three original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
On July 6, 2001, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, which took no further action on it.
The bill had 5 cosponsors and never received a floor vote; the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003, and the bill died in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The FDA's existing authority to treat foods and supplements as drugs when they make medical claims stays intact, and the supplement and food industries did not win the marketing freedom the bill would have granted. Consumers who rely on drug-approval standards for disease claims are in the same position as before.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The FDA and current evidence standards

for.name: Rep. Ron Paul
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Foods are not Drugs Act on June 21, 2001, to exclude food and dietary supplements from the definition of a drug.

for.name: Rep. John Hostettler and Rep. Bob Stump

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. W.J. Tauzin
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on June 21, 2001, and referred it to the Health subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing or markup for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's five cosponsors split 4 Republicans and 1 Democrat, but no committee or floor action ever produced a recorded vote, so no party-line pattern exists.

industries.note: The bill would have let them market supplements as treating or preventing disease without the clinical trials and FDA review required of drugs — a large commercial gain. Because the bill died in subcommittee, they keep operating under current rules, where medical claims trigger drug regulation.
The same change would have covered ordinary food, allowing health and disease claims on food labels without FDA drug-level evidence. No outcome change, since the bill never advanced.
